newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK monetary system to stay separate post-handover.
newsitem.headline: HK monetary system to stay separate post-handover.

text.p: Hong Kong's monetary system will remain completely independent of the People's Bank of China (PBOC) after the territory reverts to Chinese rule, Hong Kong financial officials stressed in the days before the handover.
The Hong Kong dollar shall remain Hong Kong's legal tender and be freely convertible, Joseph Yam, chief executive at the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the territory's de facto central bank, said.
Capital shall flow freely and there shall be no exchange controls, he said.

"There are no controls on money moving in and out of Hong Kong and never will be," Yam proclaimed to a group of foreign journalists trying to understand out what "one country, two systems" means for monetary management after the handover.
Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
Yam, the top official since 1993 at the monetary authority under the British colonial administration, will continue in his post when Hong Kong becomes a Special Administrative Region of China.
"I am very happy being a central banker and have no ambitions elsewhere," Yam said on Thursday.
Under the Basic Law, the territory's future constitution, Hong Kong enjoys substantial autonomy, including in the area of monetary affairs.

Article 110 of the Basic Law states that the SAR "shall, on its own, formulate monetary and financial policies, safeguard the free operation of financial business and financial markets, and regulate and supervise them in accordance with law."
What that means is that the HKMA is solely accountable to the SAR government and that the PBOC will not take the place of the HKMA and will not set up an office in Hong Kong, Yam said.
The HKMA has taken pains to ensure that international investors understand that Hong Kong's monetary management will remain separate from that of the People's Bank of China.
Over the last several months, Yam, sometimes in the company of Chen Yuan, deputy chairman of the PBOC, has travelled to the United States, Europe and other parts of Asia to spread the word.

Indeed, in an article published earlier this year in a local Hong Kong newspaper, Yam stressed that Hong Kong would enjoy a higher degree of autonomy when it returns to China as a Special Administrative Region than it ever did under British rule.

Royal Instructions presently in force state that the governor shall not assent to "any Bill affecting the Currency of the Colony or relating to the issue of Bank notes", or "any Bill establishing any Banking Association, or amending or altering the constitution, powers, or privileges of any Banking Association", without previous approval from London.

"Under the Basic Law, there is only the corresponding general requirement that laws enacted by the SAR legislature must be reported to the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress for the record," Yam said in February.

The HKMA views the maintenance of currency stability as its first policy objective. Its other goals are preserving banking stability, building market infrastructure and developing Hong Kong as an international financial centre.
The Hong Kong dollar is absolutely separate from China's currency, the renminbi.
Because the Hong Kong dollar is pegged to the U.S. unit at a rate of HK$7.80 to US$1, the monetary authority cannot influence both interest rates and the foreign exchange rate.
Hong Kong's financial leaders repeatedly have stressed that the Hong Kong dollar will remain linked to the U.S. dollar.

"For me, the continuation of the linked exchange rate is fundamental to reassuring international investors that the system in Hong Kong will remain unchanged," Financial Secretary Donald Tsang told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday.

The PBOC has said that it would use part of its ample foreign currency reserves to assist Hong Kong if its currency were to come under attack, a pledge that is in line with an Asia-wide effort toward cooperation in financial matters.
Hong Kong and China have signed a pact to aid each other in times of currency instability and each, separately, has entered into similar agreements with other Asian countries.
